sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Gyromitra esculenta bears an irregular reddish to dark chestnut-brown head with rounded, brain-like folds rather than the regular pits and sharp ridges of a true morel. Its short, often furrowed stem is pale cream to tan. It has no gills. A lengthwise cut reveals several irregular cavities between the head and stem, rather than one continuous hollow chamber. Odour varies and is not a reliable identification feature.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It appears in spring and early summer, chiefly on sandy ground in conifer woods, especially beneath pines. Size, colour and fruiting time vary by locality. The name G. esculenta may also cover a complex of closely related species, so a photograph alone cannot settle every specimen.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: True morels (Morchella species) have a more regular honeycomb of deep pits bounded by narrow ridges and are usually hollow as one continuous space when cut lengthwise. The convoluted, chambered head of Gyromitra is a warning sign. Do not rely on any single visual character to decide that a wild mushroom is safe to eat.

sections.title: Toxicity and legal context
sections.text: Gyromitrin can be converted to toxic methylhydrazine compounds. Poisoning may begin with vomiting and diarrhoea and can progress to liver injury, seizures and, rarely, death. The toxin can enter cooking vapour; boiling or drying reduces but does not completely eliminate it. France banned sale of false morels, fresh or processed, in 1991. Finland still permits sale under warnings, but its Food Authority reported in 2025 that residual toxin remains after recommended preparation and no safe intake could be established.

traits: Irregular dark reddish-brown, brain-like folded head, without honeycomb pits
Pale cream to tan, stout, often furrowed stem; no gills
Lengthwise cut shows multiple irregular cavities in the head and stem
Usually on sandy ground in conifer woods in spring to early summer
Odour varies and is not a reliable identification sign
safetyNote: Potentially deadly: do not eat Gyromitra esculenta. Gyromitrin may cause severe gastrointestinal, liver and nervous-system poisoning; cooking vapour can also be hazardous. Boiling or drying cannot guarantee safety. Seek urgent poison-centre or medical advice after ingestion.
